title: KCA Council Candidates Forum: Housing, Water & Bill 9 | Kihei

recap.headline: Kīhei Community Association forum: Kahului, Wailuku and Upcountry council races
recap.in_60_seconds: The Kīhei Community Association held a Maui County Council candidate forum in Kīhei ahead of the August 8 primary. Candidates came up in three district groups, each giving a two-minute opening statement and then answering questions in about two minutes each, with a timekeeper and no audience Q&A. Nine candidates took part: two for the Kahului seat, five for Wailuku-Waiheʻe-Waikapū and two for Upcountry. Questions covered housing affordability, flooding and runoff, reef protection, homelessness, tourism revenue, Bill 9 on short-term rentals, South Maui water supply and county reform.
recap.moderated_by: a Kīhei Community Association moderator, with a timekeeper

answers.summary: Said South Maui needs actionable solutions for water management and storm recovery, and called for prioritizing wetland conservation and beach restoration as reefs remain polluted by runoff. Said local businesses are struggling and unchecked tourism isn't the solution; supports diversifying into film and television for high-wage jobs and expanding agriculture for food sustainability.

Said he is not born and raised on Maui but has lived here about 20 years and works in IT in Wailea. Said he is running because of a growing humanitarian crisis of homelessness he sees on his commute, and also to champion affordable housing and water management, saying recent flooding could be mitigated by addressing its root cause.

questions.question: What is one specific action you would take to make housing more affordable for residents?

answers.summary: Said "affordable" gets used a lot and asked what affordable really means, saying $800,000 to $900,000 homes are not affordable for what local workers are paid.

Said he wants to stop residents moving off-island because they are priced out of paradise. Said making more units available is the bottom line, since some people on the street can't afford rent, which he called a root cause of the issue.

questions.question: Residents in Kīhei face flooding; what would you do to address flooding in South Maui?

answers.summary: Said his company planted trees upcountry, and that a zipline company explained one root cause is rainbow eucalyptus drawing water from the soil, leaving dust that turns to slurry and washes down gulches, damaging infrastructure. Proposed putting concrete down, as done in L.A. and other places with major flooding.

Said she differs from her opponent because concrete is what causes the flooding. Called for returning to the ahupuaʻa mauka-to-mākaʻi mindset, using wetlands to let water go where it needs to, and conditioning new developments on including retention basins.

questions.question: Tourism is down in Maui and the county is losing revenue; what is one revenue or cost-cutting idea you would pursue in office?

answers.summary: Supports economic diversity. Proposed the county partner with the owner of the Kahului Maui Marketplace to use the Old Sports Authority for a bowling alley and arcade for families, and use empty warehouses or storefronts as co-ops where small businesses rent stalls, so Maui doesn't always depend on tourism.
Said many costs come from taxes. Said he is not against taxing tourism but wants to make it easier for visitors to come, because tourists staying in hotels shop at local businesses and buy in bulk.

questions.question: What is one bold idea you believe Maui should consider that isn't being discussed enough?

answers.summary: Proposed building a facility to assist homeless people, saying there is plenty of space and that it could be placed in the location suggested for a bowling alley.

Said, as an advocate for the houseless, that shelters are needed but only as a temporary step. Said the long-term need is transitional housing and wraparound services to give people a hand up, not a handout.

questions.question: Why do you want to be a County Council member?

answers.summary: Said she wants to be the voice of the people and sit at the table to represent what residents think is important. Said she will listen and support whatever needs to be done to make Maui better for everyone.

Said, as an IT professional, he finds joy in helping people, such as bringing a downed network back up, and wants to bring that problem-solving mindset to county issues like housing costs and homelessness. Said people can't simply be taken off the streets into a facility, but things can be made better for them and everyone.

Said Maui needs architects, engineers and planners with foresight to go beyond one way in and one way out, noting people get stuck in traffic on Peelani Highway during flooding. Asked where the 2,000 people in upcoming South Maui project units will drive, and called for a second way in and out for each district, saying SKR is not the answer.
Thanked attendees and the hosts for the chance to speak, said this was his second time appearing in public, and said he is running because he wants to make change.

Said he has a master's in policy and planning, was a policy analyst for a legislature and city council, and developed nonprofit housing. Said he is running over affordability, with five platform areas: housing, affordable preschool, local services such as at the Kīhei Community Center, lower grocery costs and infrastructure. Said traffic is the top issue he hears in Kīhei.

Said he is 49, married with a blended family, and a certified arborist of over 20 years who oversees a tree company's Maui operation with over 30 employees, budgets and contracts. Said he is a pastor whose ministry serves a weekly meal to over 120 people facing addiction and homelessness and visits prisons, and asked for votes.

Said he is running because he sees families moving away every week at the airport, including his own daughter to Las Vegas. Said he has managed Kahului Airport for 20 years after 20 years with Hawaiian Airlines, has crisis-management experience, and has relationships with congressional, state and local officials that are key to getting support.

Said he wants to join the progressive side of the council and work with Bobby Pāʻia. Said developers bring teams of attorneys that steamroll contract negotiations and he will fight for the people, not special interests or big developers. Said he is endorsed by the Pono Network as an ʻohana candidate.

Said she is a mother from Maui whose family has been here for generations, served on the Maui Planning Commission, most recently as vice chair, and the Wailuku Redevelopment Agency, and led the Maui Historical Society. Said she is running because families are moving away, and has owned small businesses and worked in property management for over 20 years.

questions.question: Homelessness affects families, businesses and public spaces across Maui; what is one concrete action you would take as a council member to address it?

answers.summary: Said a business told him houseless people were urinating in its parking lot and the owner favored the idea of a portable toilet at another location. Proposed housing as the first answer to homelessness, both transitional and permanent.

Said mental health and drug addiction are the root, with at least 80% using drugs, and must be addressed with compassion, respect and dignity alongside churches, nonprofits and families. Said many homeless people come from the mainland, that this should stop, and those here should be sent back with compassion and dignity.

Described taking part, with the County, in cleaning up a homeless encampment on the road to Kanahā Beach Park beside the wildlife sanctuary under airport jurisdiction, an area used by beachgoers, fishermen and walkers.

Said he works with homelessness and drug addiction daily as a state public defender, and thanked Randy for helping people sent to him. Proposed declaring a houselessness emergency and housing everyone, for example in the vacant Sears building near the bus station and hospital.

Said she helped organize Kīpukau Maui, which got housing for fire survivors and houseless people, and with family and friends created a resource guide for getting identifications, social security cards and birth certificates needed for services. Proposed increasing shelter capacity, with separate places for families and individual adults, and prioritizing families.

questions.question: Stormwater runoff and wastewater pollution are major contributors to the decline of Maui's reefs; what would you do to protect the reefs?

answers.summary: Proposed planting trees and working with neighboring ranches such as Haleakalā Ranch to build water basins so runoff doesn't reach the shore. Proposed planting grass and vegetation in gulches to slow water before it reaches the reefs, in collaboration with the state, county and private owners.

Said a water scalping project collects 60 to 90,000 gallons a day of wastewater, which is treated and used for irrigation, including the airport water feature. Said similar projects could be done up the hill to catch, treat and reuse water for fire control and dust control, and that they researched other states and territories.

Said as a council legislative attorney he worked with Kelly King on an enabling wetlands bill for a map and wetland districts, which he said developers stopped. Said he signed the Our Hawaiʻi pledge against developer donations and would pass a Kīhei wetlands protection overlay zone, write development agreements that protect the community, and hold large landowners accountable.

Said the work starts with observing how development has changed waterways mauka to mākaʻi and assessing where, when and in which seasons water flows, then making a plan. Cited soil work on Molokaʻi and said South Maui must work with Upcountry on ungulates, non-native species and changing rains.

Said stormwater reaches the ocean because there are no catch basins or wetland overlay districts, and golf course runoff harms reefs most because of chemicals. Supports wetland overlay districts and catch basins, and said action is needed now after 10 years of inaction.

questions.question: Bill 9 turns thousands of short-term rentals into long-term rentals; are you for it and why, or if you are against it, what major step would you take to promote affordable housing in its place?

answers.summary: Said he is still reading Bill 9 and needs to know more, that it has pros and cons and could have had more time. Said some short-term rentals may convert to hotels, that a new council could go back to it, and that the council must work as a team for the community.

Said no law is a done deal and Bill 9 addresses short-term rentals owned by nonresidents sending money off-island. Supports its affordable-housing aim and proposed using property tax powers to reward local ownership and tax foreign ownership, plus a fund to help residents buy the homes.

Said as a planning commissioner she read thousands of pages, sat through over 24 hours of testimony and voted to support Bill 9, and stands by that vote because housing people is the priority. Said all her income comes from rentals but she has no short-term rentals on Maui, and favors creative ways to boost the economy.

Said Bill 9 came from 20 years of not creating affordable housing and he testified in favor while holding concerns. Cited Seattle adding 100,000 units without substantially lowering rents and said the bill needs a measure to keep rents lower; said most short-term rentals are owned by nonresidents.

Said the bill had good intentions but the process was rushed and pressured, and it's not fair for the guys who did everything right. Said they can revisit it to help the 15% and tax the 85% who don't live here, with locals getting housing first and Kamainas first.

questions.question: What is one idea or approach that you believe sets you apart from the other candidates?

answers.summary: Said he has 25 years of legal experience and that corporations, their attorneys and outside campaign finance are steamrolling the people. Said he would make council members Gabe Johnson, Shane Sinensee and Tamara Paltin stronger as a lawyer fighting for them, and urged voters to read campaign finance reports.

Said she is from here, with kūpuna traceable to Maui Komohana and Wailuku. Said she is a 42-year-old female and mother of a young family with 10 years of Maui County volunteering, and 10 years on the boards of the Maui Historical Society and Kekulopiilani, a Hawaiian charter and immersion school.

Said no one has yet addressed concerns of kūpuna or Kīhei traffic, which he said will worsen with 2,000 more people. Proposed expanding Maui's two community land trusts, in Lahaina and Wailuku, so people can get homes in one or two years instead of five to eight.
Said he leads ministries and work every day, is a personable people person who takes time to get to know people, and wants to keep serving Kīhei, Kula, Hāna, Lānaʻi and Molokaʻi.

Said his experience sets him apart, running an airport with its own police, fire, power and water reuse, and working with homeless programs, environmentalists and state and federal government. Said the airport and Maui Fire Department formed a public-public partnership sharing equipment and training, saving the county and state millions.

Said he has been retired three years and has five children and seven grandchildren. Cited research that 53% of local families no longer live here, and said his daughter's family moved to Vegas and his brother's family to Utah; said he is running to represent and serve the people.

Said he has lived in Hawaiʻi all his life and on Maui for 45 years, has farmed kalo for 40 years, and has been married 49 years. Said he always voted but had only complained from the sidelines, and is running mainly because of the growing number of people leaving Hawaiʻi.

questions.question: Central and South Maui share a water system at 98 percent capacity, South Maui has been on water restrictions for over a year and thousands of new homes are planned; what is one thing you would do to address the shortage, end restrictions and ensure smart development?

answers.summary: Said there is no single fix and the situation stems from bad management from the beginning. Said infrastructure, including water, roads and hospitals, must be built up before further growth or decisions are made.

Proposed growing more trees and said South Maui wells need care because sustainable aquifer yields aren't well understood and the capacity formula is outdated given changed weather and recharge. Said the tourism industry in South Maui uses a lot of water and communities are not at the front of the line.

questions.question: What is one reform Maui County urgently needs, and how would you begin to implement it in your first year?

answers.summary: Said corporate and special interests dictate policy in Hawaiʻi and Maui County. Said his platform is civic engagement, because people have lost trust, feel unheard and don't vote, letting corporate donations dominate; proposed a marketing and advertising campaign and education to engage residents.
Said many reforms are needed but the biggest is the nine council members holding each other accountable for their decisions.

questions.question: Residents in Kīhei face flooding that often begins Upcountry; what would you prioritize to address it?

answers.summary: Said houses were built in wetlands and that mistake must be corrected by fixing infrastructure. Said professionals should pull the data together and the nine council members should focus on redoing infrastructure to eliminate these issues.

Said flooding is a mauka-to-mākaʻi issue; drawing on work with NRCS, proposed swales and retention basins, partnerships with major landowners, and studying approaches from other countries. Said the mayor's office cited insurance and liability issues, but he believes the engineering capacity exists.

questions.question: On affordable housing, what is one thing you would focus on or try to accomplish?

answers.summary: Said housing has been built according to supply rather than for local working people. Proposed building homes according to demand by income tier for the working class, and creating policy so developers build those homes despite lower profit margins.

Proposed that county, state and federal governments build infrastructure before development and take on that cost so developers cannot pass it on. Said infrastructure is key to doing things correctly and proactively.
